tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Brass: the editing reference, compact

Brass is written by models and reviewed by people. The facts a reviewer needs sit in declarations: what a function may reach, what it requires, what it promises. Plan an edit from declarations; open a body only when they do not say what you need. When you change a type or refinement, find every declaration that uses it; a refinement shared by two functions changes both. Open `system.brass` when an entry point's access parameters change.

**What checks your work in this run.** Nothing compiles, checks, or runs. Your patch is evaluated after you finish.

## Sentences, not words

| Shape | Means | Inside it |
|---|---|---|
| `type T = B where <condition>` | the values of `B` that pass the condition | `it` is the value; its fields are `it.field` |
| `fn f(params) -> T` then `before`, `after`, `example` | an operation and its obligations | `before` names parameters; `after` adds `result` |
| `if x is T then … else …` | a test that picks a branch | inside `then`, `x` counts as a `T` |
| `for x in xs` | a bounded loop | `x` is one element; `break` leaves |
| `any x in xs where cond` / `all x in xs where cond` | is at least one / every element like this? | no effects; `any` of empty is `false`, **`all` of empty is `true`** |
| `r with { field: v }` | a copy of `r` with fields changed | other fields carry over |
| `r with { status enters S }` | a copy of `r` in state `S` | only a declared edge is legal; the `when` fields of `S` must be given |
| `access A` then `allow op(…)` | an outside capability and what it offers | reached only through a parameter of type `A` |

`in` asks membership or walks a collection; `is` asks a type or an `Ok`/`Err` arm. `where` states a condition; `if` chooses. `with` changes fields; `enters` changes state along a declared edge. `after` is proven for every input; `example` is one input, tested.

## Modules

```brass
# ship/shipments.brass
module ship.shipments
import ship.ids as ids

interface
  type Weight   = Int where it in 1 to 50000
  type Shipment = { id: ids.ShipmentId, weight: Weight, fragile: Bool, status: ShipmentStatus }
  fn grams_over(s: Shipment, ceiling: Weight) -> Int
    after result == s.weight - ceiling
private
  fn is_heavy(s: Shipment) -> Bool
body
  fn grams_over(s, ceiling) = s.weight - ceiling
  fn is_heavy(s) = s.weight >= 20000
```

- One module per file: `interface` (public), optional `private`, then `body`. Write `interface` and `body` even when empty. A function is declared once with types; its body repeats the names without types. A body with no declaration, or a declaration with no body, is a rejection.
- Every import has an alias and every imported name goes through it: `ids.ShipmentId`, never `ShipmentId`. No two imports share an alias; imports do not cycle. No versions on `module` or `import`.
- `type ShipmentId = Text` names an existing type. `Text` has `length`: `type Note = Text where it.length in 1 to 200`.
- Types and constructors start uppercase, everything else lowercase. Keywords are never names (not `to`, not `in`). `system`, `requires`, `grants`, `limit` are keywords only in the system file.
- A declaration continues onto the next line while a `(`, `<`, or `{` it opened is still open, as in Python; indentation inside does not matter.
- A record literal names every field: `{ id: id, weight: w, fragile: false, status: ShipmentStatus.Packed }`.
- **Authority is a parameter.** A function reaches outside only through an access it was handed. No access parameter, no effect.

## Conditions

```brass
type Ready = Shipment where it.status in {ShipmentStatus.Packed}
type Route = { origin: ids.Depot, dest: ids.Depot } where it.origin != it.dest
type Batch = Array<Shipment> where it.length in 0 to 200
type HeavyReady = Ready where it.weight >= 20000
```

- `it` is the value, and its fields are `it.field`, nesting by dots. A bare field name is a rejection: write `it.status`, not `status`. A refinement may follow a type anywhere a type is written. A refined value passes where its base is expected; a base value does not pass where the refinement is expected.
- Tests: `x in 1 to 10` (range), `x in {A, B}` (set), `x in s` (a named set), `x is T` (refinement; `x` must have `T`'s fields), `x is Ok` / `x is Err`. A state test is a set test: `s.status in {ShipmentStatus.Packed}`. `x is None` is a rejection: write `x == None`.
- A passed test narrows the name inside `then`; tests joined with `and` all narrow; `or` narrows nothing; `not` narrows nothing. In `else`, only a single test on states or on `Ok`/`Err` knows the complement. A narrowing lasts until the name is rebound.
- **Only `x is T` gives a value a named type.** Testing a field (`p.status in {…}`) lets you read what depends on it but does not make `p` a `Ready`. A `let`, argument, field, or result also holds a refinement when the checker can prove its condition there from the facts that establish a `before` (see Types and literals). A literal, a `const` name, or a `with` whose fields the checker sees satisfies a refinement directly when the condition holds.

**Contracts.**

```brass
fn postage(s: Heavy, base: Cents) -> Cents
  before base <= 1000
  after  result == base + 500
  example postage({ id: "s1", weight: 25000, fragile: false, status: ShipmentStatus.Packed }, 400) == 900
```

- `before`: what the caller must establish, by a parameter's type, a `const` fact, its own `before`, a callee's `after`, or a test on the path. `after`: what holds on success; on `Outcome<T>` it speaks of the value inside `Ok`, named `result`. Several `before` lines hold together.
- A condition may use `+`, `-`, `*` by a constant or of bounded values, `/` and `%` by a nonzero constant, comparisons, `in`, `not`, `and`, `or`, parameters, `result`, fields, `const` names, `length`. No calls, no quantifiers, no floats. "When p then q" is `not (p) or q`. At one level of parentheses use `and` or `or`, never both. The left side of `and` holds while the right is checked.
- A caller's clause that depends on a callee with no contract cannot be proven: the remedy is a contract on the callee.
- `example f(args) == value`: one concrete call, run by `check`. Only on a total `fn` with no access parameter; the arguments must satisfy the types and every `before`. Tested, never proven.
- **Tiers.** Proven: every contract on a Brass function, unless it is proved from an enforced fact. Enforced by the runtime: an access's reserved bounds and authority checks, every reply from outside, an entry point's parameter types and `before` lines at the boundary. Assumed: nothing checks it. Only proven is a guarantee.

## Bodies

A body is lines run top to bottom; the last line is the value. `and`/`or` stop at the first operand that decides them.

```brass
fn total_weight(batch) =
  let total: Int = 0
  for s in batch
    total = total + s.weight
  total
```

- Every `let` names its type. An unread `let`, or a value computed and dropped (unless it is `Done`, as in `store.save(x)?` on its own line), is a rejection. Parameters and loop variables cannot be rebound. A branch that does not rebind a name leaves its old value. Rebinding gives the name a new value; the old value is unchanged, as every value is.
- `if c then a else b` is a value (both branches); `if c then x = x + 1` on its own line is a step and needs no `else`. A branch may be an indented block whose last line is its value.

# Task C: cash advances

## Requirement

Field staff cannot front the cost of a trip. Before a trip, a staff member may request a cash advance for a period, and settle it against the expense report they file afterwards.

- **Requesting.** An active staff member requests an advance for a period that is not closed, stating the amount (at least 1 cent). The advance belongs to the staff member's department.
- **Approving.** An advance is approved by the same people, in the same order, as an expense report of that amount from that staff member would be, with the same refusals: not by the requester, not in a closed period, not by anyone but the required approver, and at the last step not past the department's budget unless the approver is Finance. An approved advance counts against the department's budget for its period, like an approved report.
- **Paying.** Finance pays an approved advance through the ledger, in full, with the advance's id as the key.
- **Settling.** When Finance pays an expense report, they may settle it against one of the staff member's paid advances: the report's payment is reduced by the advance. If the advance covers the whole report, nothing is paid through the ledger, the report takes the advance's ledger reference, and the difference is recorded on the advance as owed by the staff member. Either way the advance is settled and the report is paid. An advance can be settled once, only against an approved report by the same staff member in the same period; otherwise Conflict.
- **Budget.** An advance counts against its department's budget for its period while Approved or Paid. Once settled it stops counting, since the report it was settled against counts instead.
- **Outstanding.** An advance paid but not settled within two periods of its period is outstanding: `period + 2 < today`.
- Every state change of an advance is audited like a report's: each approval step, the payment, and the settlement. Requesting one is not audited, as opening a draft is not.

## Interface

**Advance:** id, badge, department, period, amount, status, approvals (as a report's), reference (once paid), owed (once settled; 0 when the report covered it). Status: Requested → Approved → Paid → Settled. Advances are not rejected in this change.

An advance is paid like a report: a closed period does not block it.

New entry points:

```
request_advance(badge, period, amount) → advance id
approve_advance(advance_id, approver) → the advance's status after
pay_advance(advance_id, finance_badge) → ledger reference
pay_against(report_id, advance_id, finance_badge) → ledger reference, or "settled" when nothing was paid
outstanding_advances(today) → list of advance ids, in the store's order
```

**Statement:** spend and remaining include counted advances; after the report rows, one row per counted advance, in the store's order, with `total` and `budgeted` its amount.

**Store** gains `advance(id)`, `advances_for(department, period)` (every advance there, at most 1,000), `paid_advances()` (every Paid advance, at most 1,000), `save_advance(advance)`. `next_id()` supplies advance ids. Audit entries for an advance use the advance's id in the report field.

## Acceptance

The same hidden cases run against both implementations. They check results; every advance and report saved (status, approvals, reference, owed); every audit entry; every ledger call; that spend and the statement include approved and paid advances; and that everything the baseline already does is unchanged.

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
 - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds

  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

14	  fn add_line(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge, line: lines.Line) -> Outcome<Done>
15	  fn submit(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Done>
16	  fn approve(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<reports.ReportStatus>
17	  fn reject(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge, reason: ids.Reason) -> Outcome<Done>
18	  fn request_changes(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge, reason: ids.Reason) -> Outcome<Done>
19	  fn resubmit(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Done>
20	
21	  fn may_act(store: host.Store, r: reports.Submitted, who: staff.Active) -> Outcome<Bool>
22	private
23	  type Gate = { r: reports.Submitted, who: staff.Active }
24	  type Own  = { r: reports.Report, who: staff.Active }
25	
26	  fn gate(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Gate>
27	  fn own(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Own>
28	  fn open_and_valid(store: host.Store, r: reports.Report) -> Outcome<Done>
29	  fn required_for(store: host.Store, r: reports.Submitted) -> Outcome<Maybe<ids.Badge>>
30	  fn stand_in(store: host.Store, required: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Maybe<ids.Badge>>
31	  fn final_approval(store: host.Store, r: reports.Submitted, who: staff.Active) -> Outcome<reports.ReportStatus>
32	body
33	  fn open_draft(store, badge, period, first_line) =
34	    let who: staff.Staff = store.staff(badge)?
35	    if who is staff.Active then
36	      let closed: Bool = store.period_closed(period)?
37	      if not closed then
38	        let id: ids.ReportId = store.next_id()?
39	        store.save_report({ id: id, badge: badge, department: who.department, period: period, lines: [first_line], status: reports.ReportStatus.Draft, approvals: [] })?
40	        Ok(id)
41	      else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the period is closed")
42	    else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "staff member is not active")
43	
44	  fn add_line(store, report_id, badge, line) =
45	    let o: Own = own(store, report_id, badge)?
46	    if o.r is reports.Editable then
47	      if o.r.lines.length < 50 then store.save_report(reports.add_line(o.r, line))
48	      else Err(FailureCode.InvalidInput, "a report holds at most 50 lines")
49	    else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the report is not editable")
50	
51	  fn submit(store, report_id, badge) =
52	    let o: Own = own(store, report_id, badge)?
53	    if o.r is reports.Draft then
54	      open_and_valid(store, o.r)?
55	      store.save_report(reports.submit(o.r))?
56	      store.append_audit(audit.entry(badge, o.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Draft, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, "submitted"))
57	    else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the report is not a draft")
58	
59	  fn resubmit(store, report_id, badge) =
60	    let o: Own = own(store, report_id, badge)?
61	    if o.r is reports.AwaitingChanges then
62	      open_and_valid(store, o.r)?
63	      store.save_report(reports.resubmit(o.r))?
64	      store.append_audit(audit.entry(badge, o.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.ChangesRequested, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, "resubmitted"))
65	    else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the report is not awaiting changes")
66	
67	  fn approve(store, report_id, approver) =
68	    let g: Gate = gate(store, report_id, approver)?
69	    if g.r.approvals.length + 1 >= routing.steps_for(lines.total(g.r.lines)) then final_approval(store, g.r, g.who)
70	    else
71	      store.save_report(reports.add_approval(g.r, g.who.badge))?
72	      store.append_audit(audit.entry(g.who.badge, g.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, "approved; awaiting the next approver"))?
73	      Ok(reports.ReportStatus.Submitted)
74	
75	  fn reject(store, report_id, approver, reason) =
76	    let g: Gate = gate(store, report_id, approver)?
77	    store.save_report(reports.reject(g.r))?
78	    store.append_audit(audit.entry(g.who.badge, g.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, reports.ReportStatus.Rejected, reason))
79	
80	  fn request_changes(store, report_id, approver, reason) =
81	    let g: Gate = gate(store, report_id, approver)?

module desk.payment
import desk.ids as ids
import desk.lines as lines
import desk.staff as staff
import desk.reports as reports
import desk.audit as audit
import desk.host as host

interface
  fn pay(store: host.Store, ledger: host.Ledger, report_id: ids.ReportId, finance_badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Text>
  fn close_period(store: host.Store, period: ids.Period, finance_badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Done>
body
  fn pay(store, ledger, report_id, finance_badge) =
    let who: staff.Staff = store.staff(finance_badge)?
    if who is staff.Finance then
      let r: reports.Report = store.report(report_id)?
      if r is reports.Approved then
        let reference: Text = ledger.pay(r.badge, lines.total(r.lines), r.id)?
        store.save_report(reports.pay(r, reference))?
        store.append_audit(audit.entry(who.badge, r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Approved, reports.ReportStatus.Paid, "paid"))?
        Ok(reference)
      else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the report is not approved")
    else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "only active finance staff may pay")

  fn close_period(store, period, finance_badge) =
    let who: staff.Staff = store.staff(finance_badge)?
    if who is staff.Finance then
      let closed: Bool = store.period_closed(period)?
      if closed then Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the period is already closed")
      else store.close_period(period)
    else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "only active finance staff may close a period")

# desk/queries.brass
module desk.queries
import desk.ids as ids
import desk.lines as lines
import desk.staff as staff
import desk.reports as reports
import desk.host as host
import desk.budget as budget
import desk.review as review

interface
  type Ids       = Array<ids.ReportId> where it.length in 0 to 1000
  type Row       = { id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge, status: reports.ReportStatus, total: Int, budgeted: Int }
  type Rows      = Array<Row> where it.length in 0 to 1000
  type Statement = { department: ids.DepartmentId, period: ids.Period, budget: ids.Money, spend: Int, remaining: Int, rows: Rows }

  fn statement(store: host.Store, department: ids.DepartmentId, period: ids.Period) -> Outcome<Statement>

  fn spend(store: host.Store, department: ids.DepartmentId, period: ids.Period) -> Outcome<Int>
  fn pending_for(store: host.Store, approver: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Ids>
body
  fn spend(store, department, period) =
    let dept: staff.Department = store.department(department)?
    let rs: reports.Reports = store.reports_for(dept.id, period)?
    Ok(budget.spend_of(rs))

  fn statement(store, department, period) =
    let dept: staff.Department = store.department(department)?
    let rs: reports.Reports = store.reports_for(dept.id, period)?
    let rows: Rows = []
    for r in rs
      if r is reports.Counted then rows = rows ++ [{ id: r.id, badge: r.badge, status: r.status, total: lines.total(r.lines), budgeted: lines.budgeted_total(r.lines) }]
    let spent: Int = budget.spend_of(rs)
    Ok({ department: dept.id, period: period, budget: dept.budget, spend: spent, remaining: dept.budget - spent, rows: rows })

  fn pending_for(store, approver) =
    let who: staff.Staff = store.staff(approver)?
    let rs: reports.Reports = store.submitted_reports()?
    let out: Ids = []
    if who is staff.Active then
      for r in rs
        if r is reports.Submitted and r.badge != who.badge then
          let verdict: Outcome<Bool> = review.may_act(store, r, who)
          if verdict is Ok then
            let allowed: Bool = verdict?
            if allowed then out = out ++ [r.id]
    Ok(out)
